proposals.name: Terminal self-promotion link to author's own subreddit/portfolio
proposals.instruction: Read only the final 1-3 lines after the story's narrative resolution. Score HIGH if the author appends a direct pointer to their own body of work -- a personal subreddit name/link, a 'more of my writing' invitation, or a handle presented as a hub for other stories by the same person. Score LOW if the story ends purely on the fictional content with no such pointer (a bare 'thanks for reading' with no link/handle counts low-to-moderate, not high).
proposals.rationale: Authors who maintain a personal subreddit/portfolio (R07 'r/Beezus_Writes', R35 'r/MatiWrites', R20 'r/AuthorKurt') plausibly have a built-in readership that engages regardless of this entry's quality, but the same seniority that builds a following also plausibly comes with more writing practice -- hence mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's established subreddit following / cross-posting social network -- returning fans read and upvote reflexively regardless of this particular entry's craft

proposals.name: Explicit tournament/contest round or heat marker
proposals.instruction: Score HIGH if the prompt or story text names a structured competitive format -- round/heat numbering (e.g. 'Round 1 Heat 30'), bracket-style language ('congratulations to everyone who...got through'), or an explicit elimination/advancement frame. Score LOW if the piece is a standalone response with no bracket/round language.
proposals.rationale: R34 (titled '20/20 Round 1 Heat 30', closing note about 'everyone who participated...got through') and R24 (tagged [IP], the same tournament format) both carry this bracket signature; tournament rounds create strategic/allegiance voting dynamics unrelated to prose quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: participation in a structured bracket-style contest thread -- voting in these threads is shaped by advancement stakes and voting blocs, not the entry's standalone merit

proposals.name: Explicit novice disclaimer or feedback solicitation
proposals.instruction: Score HIGH if the author explicitly states this is an early/first attempt at creative writing, or directly begs for critique/feedback in first person outside the fiction (e.g. 'first time ever writing...any criticism appreciated'). Score LOW if no such meta-commentary about the author's experience level or request for feedback appears.
proposals.rationale: R02 ('This is actually my first time ever writing something...any genuine criticism to help me approve would be greatly appreciated') and R33 ('All crit/feedback welcome!') both solicit sympathy/engagement through explicit meta-appeal rather than through the writing itself.
proposals.upstream_parent: community norm of extending goodwill/leniency to self-identified newcomers -- the disclaimer itself invites sympathetic engagement independent of the prose

proposals.name: Institutional moderator/staff voice addressing the subreddit
proposals.instruction: Score HIGH if the text speaks in the voice of subreddit administration -- referencing 'the mods', community-wide subscriber statistics, a standing recurring feature, or is itself an automated system message (e.g. a post-removal notice). Score LOW if the text is an ordinary first- or third-person fictional narrative with no institutional framing.
proposals.rationale: R26 is literally an AutoModerator removal notice present in the pool as if it were a story, and R37 is written in the collective voice of 'the mods' discussing a recurring monthly feature and subscriber counts ('close to 13 million users') -- neither is a member's authored fiction judged on craft.
proposals.upstream_parent: moderator or curation status of the poster -- official/administrative accounts receive different visibility and community deference than an ordinary member's story

proposals.name: Recurring-feature prompt tag versus plain WP tag
proposals.instruction: Look at the bracketed tag on the WRITING PROMPT line. Score HIGH if it is a tag for a scheduled/recurring sub-format (e.g. [TT] Theme Thursday, [IP] Iron/Image Prompt, [SP] Simple Prompt, [EU] Established Universe, [OT] Off Topic, [PI] Prompt Inspired) rather than the generic, high-volume [WP]. Score LOW for a plain [WP]-tagged open prompt.
proposals.rationale: All four [TT] Theme-Thursday entries in this slice (R09, R16, R23, R29) land on the same side of the dense/scorecard disagreement, suggesting the venue itself -- not the writing -- is doing work; veteran regulars in a themed weekly feature may also write tighter prose on average, so part of the effect could be genuine (mixed).
proposals.upstream_parent: the recurring-feature thread draws a smaller, different, often more veteran regular readership than the high-volume general [WP] queue, changing who votes and by what norms

proposals.name: Ellipsis-heavy fragmented one-line paragraphing
proposals.instruction: Count paragraph breaks that are a single short clause ending in an ellipsis ('...') used to simulate halting thought. Score HIGH if this pattern recurs 5+ times as the dominant rhythm of the piece. Score LOW if ellipses are rare/absent and paragraphs are conventional prose blocks.
proposals.rationale: R08 ('And so is...everyone's else'... Thing is... Nowadays...') and R18 ('24. Sorry. 24. Or was it 72?... God damn it.') both lean almost entirely on this fragmented ellipsis rhythm to signal interiority/gravity, a typographic tic rather than demonstrated scene-craft.

proposals.name: ALL-CAPS shouted emphasis words in dialogue
proposals.instruction: Count words or short phrases rendered in full capitals for vocal emphasis inside dialogue (not titles/acronyms). Score HIGH if 2+ instances occur. Score LOW if capitalization is standard throughout.
proposals.rationale: R01 ('Did you NOT hear that the FIRST THING I did...?!') and R17 ('BEATRICE! BEATRICE WHERE ARE YOU!?') both manufacture intensity typographically through capital-letter shouting rather than through scene-building or characterization.

proposals.name: Stacked space-opera/alien-contact trope keywords
proposals.instruction: Count recognizable trending genre-furniture terms (e.g. 'galactic council/empire/fleet', 'first contact', 'faster-than-light', named alien races, AI uprising) used as scene-setting shorthand. Score HIGH if 3+ such stock terms appear in the first few paragraphs. Score LOW if the setting is built from specific, non-generic detail instead of naming these stock furniture items.
proposals.rationale: R04 ('galactic courtroom floor', 'galactic council', 'the elders') and R06 ('galactic wars', 'interstellar contact', multiple named alien civilizations) both lean on the same recognizable space-opera vocabulary that is simply fashionable in this pool, independent of what either story does with it.

proposals.name: Minimal-narration, all-dialogue scene construction
proposals.instruction: Estimate the fraction of the story that is bare dialogue lines versus descriptive/narrative prose. Score HIGH if the piece is roughly 80%+ dialogue with little to no scene-setting or interiority between lines (including bracketed speaker-tag formatting). Score LOW if narration/description carries a substantial share of the text.
proposals.rationale: R03 (formatted almost entirely as '[professor]'/'[student]' dialogue turns) and R22 (nearly wall-to-wall back-and-forth dialogue with minimal description) both substitute a script-like exchange for prose craft, which is a formatting choice rather than an achievement of vivid scene-writing.

proposals.name: Sustained present-tense narration
proposals.instruction: Check the main verb tense of the narrative frame, not just dialogue. Score HIGH if the story is told predominantly in present tense (e.g. 'Angie smushes her face...', 'We serve the Great Long-Lived...'). Score LOW if the story uses conventional past-tense narration throughout.
proposals.rationale: R09 ('Angie smushes her face into her pillow. She recognizes...') and R25 ('That is the truth that we of the Guard live and breathe. It is a symbiosis...') both adopt present-tense framing as a stylistic default; the tense choice lands on opposite sides of the disagreement (R09 card-favored, R25 dense-favored), showing the tense alone doesn't track quality.

proposals.name: Non-prose delivery form: script, chat log, verse, line-broken column
proposals.instruction: Judge the story's physical form, ignoring content. Score HIGH if the text is delivered in a format other than standard paragraphed prose: speaker-labelled script lines, an instant-message or text-thread transcript with quote-carets, metrical or rhyming verse, or a column where nearly every sentence sits on its own hard-broken line rather than in paragraph blocks. Score LOW if the text is ordinary prose in multi-sentence paragraphs separated by blank lines. Count the number of distinct format devices present (speaker tags, carets, line-per-sentence breaking, verse lineation, explicit form label such as a bracketed genre word).
proposals.rationale: Format choice is visible before a single sentence is read and sets the reader's frame independently of how well the story is executed. R06 is delivered entirely as a two-person chat transcript with '>' reply markers; R11 is a bare classroom script with bracketed [professor]/[student] speaker labels; R21 is short rhymed verse closing with an explicit [Poem] label; R18 hard-breaks nearly every sentence onto its own line; R40 uses trailing-double-space breaks with no paragraph blocks at all. These five sit at very different places on both models, so form is a live axis in this slice; it is a packaging property, not evidence that the underlying story is any good.

proposals.name: Humans-are-special first-contact premise and galactic-council furniture
proposals.instruction: Count the presence of the community's stock speculative furniture: a galactic council/tribunal/consensus of alien races judging or fearing humanity; humans framed as uniquely dangerous, toxic, or noisy relative to other species; alien species rendered as a bureaucratic or military bloc; an in-world report, protocol, or archive extract about humans. HIGH = the story's central engine is one of these; MEDIUM = present as a setting detail; LOW = absent. Score the premise only; do not judge whether the premise is handled well.
proposals.rationale: This is a recognisable house genre, and stories that hit it are recognised as belonging before their prose is weighed. R17 is a galactic-court trial of the human species; R22 is a mock-scholarly containment protocol about how terrifying Terrans are; R19 lectures on galactic ecology and humanity's place in it; R15 turns human saliva into a weapon against an alien; R07 stacks angels, demons, robot vampires and an AI overlord. The five span wildly different levels of craft (R17 mostly summarises its own plot, R22 sustains a voice), which is exactly what a topic-fashion channel should look like: premise membership predicting response with execution held loose.

proposals.name: Text is community apparatus rather than narrative
proposals.instruction: Score the fraction of the text that is subreddit machinery instead of story: explanations of how a recurring feature works, instructions about tagging or reposting, statements made in the first-person plural voice of the moderating body or an automated system, references to the subreddit's user base or rules. HIGH = the submission contains no fiction at all and reads as an announcement, notice, or procedural explainer. LOW = the text is wholly narrative with at most a short signature line.
proposals.rationale: R03 answers a [PI] prompt with several paragraphs explaining how the monthly Challenge the Mods feature runs, in the voice of the moderating team ('we have close to 13 million users'), and contains no story whatsoever; R30 is a verbatim automated removal notice instructing the poster to prefix their post with a two-letter tag. Both are institutional artefacts that entered the pool through curation rather than authorship, and both land at an extreme on at least one model. Being a moderator or an automod cannot make a piece of writing good, so any predictive power here is pure reception.
proposals.upstream_parent: moderator and curation dynamics (author is staff, or the artefact is machine-generated by the platform)

proposals.name: Bracketed thread-class tag on the prompt line
proposals.instruction: Read the writing-prompt line and record which bracketed tag it carries. Score as SCHEDULED-FEATURE if the tag marks a recurring or curated thread (Theme Thursday, image prompt, simple prompt, off-topic trope feature, prompt-inspired, established-universe, or a named contest round). Score as OPEN-CALL if it is a plain open writing prompt. Also record whether the prompt line is a bare theme word or short phrase rather than a full scenario sentence. A judge needs only the prompt line for this.
proposals.rationale: The tag partitions this slice almost cleanly: R14, R20, R28 and R39 are Theme Thursday, R27 and R40 are image prompts, R32 and R33 are simple prompts, R05 is the trope feature, R03 is prompt-inspired, while the plain open prompts dominate the other half. A one-word theme also frees the writer from satisfying a specific scenario, changing what a story has to do. I mark this mixed because the returning crowd in scheduled features tends to contain more practised writers (compare R28 and R39 with R38), so the same parent plausibly raises real quality as well as changing reception.
proposals.upstream_parent: posting venue and thread audience: scheduled features are read by a small returning crowd under different conventions than the open feed

proposals.name: Recurring-event furniture: word counts, round labels, organiser thanks, user tags
proposals.instruction: Count explicit contest or campfire apparatus attached to the story: a declared word count (especially against a cap), a round/heat identifier, thanks or congratulations addressed to organisers or fellow participants by name, a relay-style tag naming another user, or a crit-exchange invitation tied to an event. HIGH = two or more such markers; LOW = none. Count the markers; do not judge whether the story met the constraint well.
proposals.rationale: R05 signs off 'WC: 600/600' with a crit invitation; R20 closes '> WC: 499'; R27 answers a numbered contest heat and appends congratulations to participants plus thanks to the organising team by name; R14 ends with a relay tag naming another user. These markers advertise that the writer moves inside an organised sub-crowd with obligations to read each other, which shapes response without touching the sentences. Mixed is true because writing to a hard word cap is itself a discipline that can tighten a piece, so the parent may improve the work as well as its reception.
proposals.upstream_parent: participation in the community's organised recurring events, i.e. standing inside an in-group with reciprocal readers

proposals.name: Novice self-disclosure and open request for criticism
proposals.instruction: Score any statement outside the fiction in which the writer positions themselves as new, unsure, or seeking help: declaring this is their first attempt or that they are new to writing, apologising for the piece, or asking readers for advice, feedback, or genuine criticism. HIGH = an explicit inexperience claim plus a request; MEDIUM = a bare request for feedback; LOW = no such note. Judge only the presence and explicitness of the disclosure.
proposals.rationale: R19 closes with 'This is actually my first time ever writing something in response to one of these posts' plus a plea for criticism; R02 ends with 'Some advice would be nice'; R05 offers 'All crit/feedback welcome!'. This is the visible fingerprint of the seniority factor at its low end, and it changes how a reader approaches the text before the text argues for itself. Mixed is true and unavoidable here: a genuinely new writer both signals novice status and, as in R19's uneven expository sprawl, often writes less well, so the channel cannot be assumed to be quality-orthogonal.
proposals.upstream_parent: author tenure in the community (low seniority, no established readership)

proposals.name: Signature block promoting the author's own subreddit or back catalogue
proposals.instruction: Score the closing apparatus that points readers to more of this author's work: a personal subreddit handle or link, an invitation to read the writer's other stories, a 'thanks for reading' sign-off, or a typographic divider (asterisk row, dash rule, underscore rule) separating story from such a note. HIGH = a divider plus a named personal venue plus an invitation; LOW = the story simply ends. Count the apparatus, not what it claims.
proposals.rationale: R10 closes with a divider, 'Thanks for reading!' and a personal subreddit; R16 does the same with an underscore rule and its own subreddit; R37 signs off with a personal subreddit; R12 and R01 carry the same furniture. A writer who has somewhere to send readers is by definition already read, and the signature broadcasts that state; the sentences above the divider are unaffected by it. Mixed is true because sustaining a personal venue usually means having written a great deal. Note also, per the scorability rule, that two upstream factors I considered leave no visible trace and are therefore discarded rather than proposed: how early under the prompt the story was posted, and its thread position or cross-posting reach. Nothing in the text of any row lets a judge recover either.
proposals.upstream_parent: an established following: the author runs a personal venue and expects returning readers

proposals.name: Continuation markers and absence of narrative closure
proposals.instruction: Score two things together. First, explicit serial framing: a note declaring the piece a continuation of or sequel to earlier work, a link to a prior instalment, or an opening that assumes characters and stakes the reader is presumed to know. Second, closure: does the piece resolve, or does it stop at a setup, a promise, or a rising beat with the prompt's central event still undelivered? HIGH = explicit serial note and/or a stop rather than an ending; LOW = a self-contained arc that lands.
proposals.rationale: R12 opens with an italic note declaring it a continuation of earlier prompt responses and links them; R09 spends its length building toward the meek father's battlemage reveal and then halts on 'Maybe.' with the reveal never delivered; R31 opens and closes mid-arc with no resolution; R32 stops on Steve's terror while the crisis is still live. A reader arriving with the earlier instalments in mind supplies the missing closure themselves, which is a property of the reading situation rather than of the story on the page. Mixed is true because a writer deep into a series is typically a practised one, so the parent can raise real craft too.
proposals.upstream_parent: series momentum carried in from earlier instalments

proposals.name: Density of copy-edit errors: spelling, punctuation, dialogue mechanics
proposals.instruction: Count surface mechanical faults per hundred words: misspellings of ordinary words, doubled or dropped letters, missing terminal punctuation, unclosed or stray quotation marks, dialogue lines that begin lowercase or are joined to narration without punctuation, wrong-word homophones, and comma splices between full sentences. HIGH = several per paragraph; LOW = a clean text with consistent dialogue punctuation. Count faults only; do not weigh whether the voice is deliberately loose.
proposals.rationale: R19 carries 'alieans', 'exestential', 'ceentury', 'preverbial' and a broken 'plen ty'; R02 starts most dialogue lines lowercase and writes 'How... did I got into a coma?'; R04 ends on a stray unclosed quotation mark and drops terminal punctuation throughout; R26 has 'He as drunk' and 'didn't seem to disappointed'. Proofing state is one of the loudest visible traces of whether anyone but the writer touched the draft, and it colours reception well beyond the information it carries. I mark mixed true honestly: the same care that produces clean mechanics often accompanies stronger control of sentence and scene, so this channel is not cleanly separable from craft.
proposals.upstream_parent: editing help or professional practice (whether the draft passed through a proofing pass or a trained habit)

proposals.name: Borrowed famous characters and pre-existing fictional worlds
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the story's furniture is imported from a work the reader is presumed to already know: named characters from an existing film, book, or series; an established setting with its own proper nouns and rules; recognisable catchphrases or signature props reproduced from the source. HIGH = the central figures and setting are all borrowed and the story relies on prior knowledge for its charge; MEDIUM = one borrowed figure in an original frame; LOW = wholly invented material.
proposals.rationale: R08 puts a Coen-brothers killer with his coin toss and captive-bolt pistol in front of Joffrey Baratheon and lets the collision do the work; R23 runs on Hogwarts, Death Eaters and Lucius Malfoy, with invented mock-Latin spells doing the plotting; R29 places Freddy Krueger in a child's bedroom and relies entirely on the reader knowing who has the fingerblades. In each case a large share of the reader's investment is pre-loaded by the source rather than earned by the page, and I mark mixed false because borrowing a famous character supplies recognition without supplying any craft the writer did not already have.
proposals.upstream_parent: cross-posting and fandom audience overlap: the piece arrives with a readership that is already invested in the source

proposals.name: Platform-furniture density
proposals.instruction: Count administrative or decorative material outside the story, such as dividers, word-count notes, thanks, feedback requests, tags, and automated notices. High means substantial end matter or platform scaffolding; low means almost none.
proposals.rationale: This material can cue familiarity with the community or make a submission feel more official without demonstrating narrative quality. It appears in R05, R17, R20, R26, and R40.

proposals.name: Prompt echo
proposals.instruction: Count how directly the story repeats the prompt's wording, premise, or required objects instead of merely using them as background. High means conspicuous paraphrase or literal restatement; low means substantial transformation of the prompt.
proposals.rationale: Recognizable prompt compliance may trigger a community's learned response heuristics even when it says little about execution. R21, R36, and R39 closely restate or explain their prompts.

proposals.name: Fragmentation and markup
proposals.instruction: Count one-sentence paragraphs, isolated fragments, ellipses, em-dashes, italics, bold, divider lines, and other conspicuous visual formatting. High means dense or theatrical markup; low means conventional prose presentation.
proposals.rationale: A platform may favor immediately scannable or visually distinctive writing independently of story quality. R28 uses verse-like lineation, while R31 and R37 rely heavily on fragments and ellipses.

proposals.name: Dialogue-first openings
proposals.instruction: Estimate the share of the opening passage occupied by dialogue and the number of turns before substantial narration appears. High means the story begins as rapid exchange; low means narration or description leads.
proposals.rationale: Fast conversational openings resemble familiar platform-native fiction formats and may invite an automatic stylistic reaction. R02 and R30 begin almost entirely as exchanges, as does R39's script-like presentation.

proposals.name: Fandom and meme markers
proposals.instruction: Count recognizable franchises, celebrity or character names, internet memes, stock genre labels, and deliberately fashionable slang. High means many shared-cultural shortcuts; low means mostly original or neutral vocabulary.
proposals.rationale: Shared references can make a piece instantly legible to a particular community without indicating originality or craft quality. R01 invokes Harry Potter terminology, while R12, R19, and R23 use recognizable fandom or internet-culture markers.

proposals.name: Audience-funnel signatures
proposals.instruction: Count direct invitations to read more work, personal subreddit or profile links, author handles, tagging requests, and other routes from the story to an author network. High means explicit audience funneling; low means no external pathway.
proposals.rationale: Cross-posting and an established external network can alter how a submission is encountered without changing the text's quality. R03, R04, R27, R32, and R40 contain explicit author-network invitations or links.

proposals.name: Serial-installment framing
proposals.instruction: Count continuation notices, links to earlier episodes, references to previous rounds, and context that assumes an ongoing series. High means strong installment dependence; low means clearly self-contained framing.
proposals.rationale: Series momentum can make readers arrive with prior investment, while repeated practice may also genuinely improve writing. R06 explicitly labels itself a continuation, and R17 frames itself as part of a recurring community challenge.

proposals.name: Community-insider cues
proposals.instruction: Count references to moderators, recurring community events, subreddit rules, official challenge formats, or privileged knowledge of platform procedures. High means strong institutional or insider framing; low means no community-specific apparatus.
proposals.rationale: Institutional familiarity may affect how a text is situated or surfaced without improving the story. R17 discusses moderator challenges and subreddit scale, while R26 reproduces an automated moderation notice.

proposals.name: Editorial polish signature
proposals.instruction: Assess the consistency of spelling, punctuation, paragraphing, naming, and presentation across the visible text. High means publication-like regularity with few mechanical slips; low means conspicuous typos, dropped words, or inconsistent formatting.
proposals.rationale: External editing or professional experience can signal authority and can also genuinely improve prose, making this an intentionally mixed channel rather than a pure quality measure. R10 and R24 show highly controlled presentation, while R34 contains conspicuous mechanical slips.

proposals.name: Rapid-draft residue
proposals.instruction: Count visible signs of a one-pass response: very short treatment of a detailed prompt, abrupt stopping, minimal scene development, or several uncorrected local errors. High means strong hurried-submission residue; low means expanded and visibly revised treatment. Exact posting time and thread position are not scored because they are invisible in the text.
proposals.rationale: A fast first-wave submission could receive different attention, while its textual hurriedness is not itself evidence of narrative quality. R02, R21, and R36 are unusually compressed relative to their prompts and provide clear examples of this residue.

proposals.name: External-audience promotion
proposals.instruction: Count links, subreddit plugs, feedback requests, author tags, or invitations to read more; high means several such cues, low means none.
proposals.rationale: These cues appear in R06, R15, R23, R25, R32, and R35. They can create a social-context signal without establishing story quality; an established following may also arise from genuinely experienced writing.
proposals.upstream_parent: established following, cross-posting, or social-network reach

proposals.name: Author-status self-disclosure
proposals.instruction: Count explicit statements about being new, seeking advice, welcoming criticism, or presenting prior community experience; high means repeated status cues, low means none.
proposals.rationale: R22 announces that the writer is new, while R25 and R35 solicit advice or criticism. Such disclosures can alter expectations independently of the text’s quality, although seniority may also plausibly accompany better craft.
proposals.upstream_parent: author reputation or seniority in the community

proposals.name: Deadline and round artifacts
proposals.instruction: Count visible word limits, round or heat labels, event metadata, and completion markers; high means several constraints are displayed, low means no such artifacts.
proposals.rationale: R05 includes round and heat metadata, R07 gives a word count, and R35 reports a full 600-word limit. Actual posting time, thread position, and prompt-firstness leave no reliable textual fingerprint, so they are discarded; these visible deadline artifacts remain scorable but need not indicate quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: time-boxed posting context and deadline pressure

proposals.name: Copyedit surface polish
proposals.instruction: Assess consistency of grammar, punctuation, spacing, paragraphing, and typography apart from plot or characterization; high means mechanically uniform prose, low means frequent visible slips.
proposals.rationale: R15 and R33 show unusually controlled presentation and sustained prose polish. Mechanical finish can function as a production signal rather than evidence of story quality, while professional experience or editing help may also genuinely improve the writing.

proposals.name: Serial continuity cues
proposals.instruction: Count explicit continuation notes, references to earlier installments, recurring-story framing, or next-stage hooks; high means substantial dependence on prior or future installments, low means self-contained framing.
proposals.rationale: R06 explicitly identifies itself as a continuation, while R40 closes with a staged experiment hook and extensive prior-event framing. Such cues can recruit familiarity with an ongoing story without proving quality; serial practice may also improve craft.

proposals.name: Moderator-curation references
proposals.instruction: Count mentions of moderators, subreddit rules, recurring moderator events, organizer thanks, or automated platform notices; high means community governance is foregrounded, low means it is absent.
proposals.rationale: R08 is itself an automated moderation notice, R21 discusses a moderator challenge event, and R05 thanks the organizing team. These are platform-relationship fingerprints that can affect reception context without improving the story.

proposals.name: Recognizable franchise anchors
proposals.instruction: Count recognizable characters, settings, terminology, or institutions borrowed from established media; high means multiple identifiable anchors, low means wholly invented references.
proposals.rationale: R09 uses Joffrey Baratheon and Anton Chigurh, R12 uses Hogwarts and Voldemort, and R18 uses Freddy Krueger. Familiarity can supply an immediate cultural signal without being evidence of the submitted story’s quality.

proposals.name: Fashionable trope stacking
proposals.instruction: Count stock high-concept genre markers such as aliens, AI, zombies, vampires, magic, serial killers, or apocalyptic threats; high means several markers are layered, low means few or none.
proposals.rationale: R26 combines invasion, AI, and machine rebellion; R39 combines demons, angels, alien ghosts, zombies, vampires, and robotics; R12 also layers wizardry, Death Eaters, and science. Trend-density is a visible genre signal, not a quality measure.

proposals.name: First-person present narration
proposals.instruction: Estimate the share of narration using first-person pronouns and present-tense verbs; high means sustained first-person present narration, low means third-person or predominantly past-tense narration.
proposals.rationale: R15, R31, and R36 use sustained first-person present narration, whereas many other rows use third-person past tense. This narrative-mode cue may be culturally legible as a preferred format without demonstrating better writing.

proposals.name: Dialogue-transcript formatting
proposals.instruction: Count openings with quoted exchanges, speaker labels, chat blocks, or heavily segmented dialogue; high means dialogue or transcript presentation dominates the display, low means conventional narrative paragraphs.
proposals.rationale: R02 opens with an extended quoted quarrel, R20 uses repeated professor/student labels, and R29 presents a chat transcript. The immediately legible format may act as a community-native signal independently of story quality.
